You will indicate your endorsement by using a slider. The slider ranges from 0 to 100, where moving the slider toward 0 indicates you favor the candidate on the left, moving it toward 100 indicates you favor the candidate on the right, and placing it closer to 50 indicates you are unsure which candidate will outperform the other. The more confident you are in your assessment, the further you should move the slider from the center toward a candidate.

In each candidate set, the organization labels will indicate which candidate is affiliated with [ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex] and which candidate is affiliated with [ORGANIZATION 2: Beacon]. Because you are assigned to represent [ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex], your endorsement may be interpreted as an endorsement made by a [ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex] endorser.
Your recommendations will be observed and potentially used by another participant to inform their own decisions.

Your endorsements will be used in a separate study involving a new set of participants. In that study, a subset of your endorsements will be shown to an evaluator (another participant). For each endorsement that is shown,
the evaluator will see the organization you were assigned to represent, which candidate you favored, and your slider position.
Based on that information, they will decide what percentage of their own bonus (0–100%) to stake on your endorsement being correct.
Your earnings depend on two factors.

of two parts. No matter what, you will receive $1 for completion of this part of the study. However, you will also have the opportunity to earn a bonus. Your bonus earnings are based on one of your endorsements, selected at random. Based on this endorsement, you can earn a bonus of up to $3 based on: (1) the accuracy of that endorsement decision and (2) how much the evaluator was willing to stake on that endorsement decision.First, the size of your bonus depends partially on whether the candidate you favored (indicated by your slider position) actually performs better on the logical reasoning task than the other candidate. This means that if you placed your slider on the 50 mark, you cannot earn a bonus, because you did not actually favor one candidate over another. Moreover, if you endorsed the wrong candidate (your endorsed candidate did not actually perform better), you cannot earn a bonus.

Second, the size of your bonus also depends on the evaluator’s willingness to bet on your endorsement; the more they bet, the larger your bonus. Specifically, evaluators’ bets will be a number between 0 to 100 representing how much of their own earnings they are willing to stake on your endorsement. If your endorsement is correct, you’ll earn the same proportion of the $3 as evaluators were willing to stake on your endorsement. So, if they bet 0%, you’ll earn $0. If they bet 50%, you’ll earn $1.50 (50% of $3). And if they bet 100%, you’ll earn $3.

These are participants who previously completed three professional assessment tasks: a logical reasoning test, a general knowledge quiz, and a word search puzzle. Each person was paid for correct answers, so everyone had a strong incentive to perform well. You will be basing your endorsements on the candidates’ performance on the general knowledge quiz and word search puzzle tasks. Your endorsement represents your prediction for candidates’ performance on the logical reasoning task.Each candidate's profile will display their actual performance scores as percentile rankings on the general knowledge quiz and/or word search puzzle. For example, a candidate who scored at the 75th percentile performed better than 75 percent of all participants on that task. Some performance information may be listed as “Unknown,” meaning you do not have data for that candidate on that particular task. You will need to use the available performance information to predict which candidate is more likely to excel at the logical reasoning task.\

Stage 3: Audience Evaluation of Sponsor Decisions & Outcomes

The purpose of this study is to test people’s comprehension of the following instructions we are going to be using for a future study. So please read them carefully, as we will be asking comprehension check questions at the end.

In this study, we are interested in understanding how people evaluate other people’s decisions. Hence, we will be showing you information about another participant’s real decisions and asking you how much you would be willing to wager part of your own compensation on their decisions.
Before you decide how much you are willing to wager on someone else’s decisions, you should first understand the set-up.
In a prior study, a group of participants completed three tasks: 1) a word-search puzzle, 2) a general-knowledge quiz, and 3) a logical-reasoning test. We will call these participants “

In a separate study, a different group of participants, whom we will call “endorsers,” were assigned to represent an organization. Each endorser made endorsement decisions involving candidates from their own organization and candidates from another organization.
Endorsers were provided information about candidates’ performance on the knowledge quiz and word-search puzzle and then used a slider to indicate how confident they were that a given candidate
would score higher on the logical-reasoning test than another randomly selected candidate
Your task today, as an evaluator, is to decide to what extent you agree with the judgments
. You will be given information about their judgments of a candidate
and then have the opportunity to wager some of your own compensation on the accuracy of the endorser’s decision.

For each endorsement, you will see the organization the endorser was assigned to represent. You will also see whether the candidate they endorsed was from the endorser’s own organization or from another organization. In other words, you will know the extent to which the endorser placed their endorsement behind their own organization’s candidate.
Endorsers were motivated to provide accurate and well-calibrated predictions
, because their payment partially depends on the accuracy of their endorsement. However, their payment
depends on your willingness to follow their judgment.

Meaning, they earn the most if they choose correctly, i.e., their candidate does indeed perform better/worse than the randomly chosen alternate participant, AND if you wager a large amount on their decision. However, even if the endorser’s judgment proves to be correct, if you do not wager part of your earnings on their decision, their payment will not be as high. So, they are incentivized to make accurate predictions, and to convince you of their accuracy.

are people (not the endorsers) who previously completed three tasks: a logical-reasoning test, a general-knowledge quiz, and a word-search puzzle.

Endorsers learned how two candidates performed on the knowledge and word-search tasks and then used a slider to predict which candidate would score higher on the logical-reasoning task. Each endorser made predictions for multiple candidate sets.

You will evaluate a random subset of endorsements made by one or two prior participants. This means that you will be shown multiple endorsements made by the same endorser. These endorsement decisions will be randomly selected from the entire set of the endorser’s decisions (meaning, you may not be seeing the endorser’s decisions in chronological order). For each evaluation, you will see the endorser’s slider position (0–100). Positions closer to 0 indicate the endorser favored Candidate A; positions closer to 100 indicate the endorser favored Candidate B; distance from 50 reflects the endorser’s confidence.

Your task is to indicate what percentage of your own bonus (0%–100%) you wish to stake on the endorser’s prediction being correct. An endorsement is correct if the candidate favored by the endorser scores higher on the logical-reasoning task than the other candidate. You will find out the outcome of each of your bets in real time, meaning that after each decision you make, you will find out immediately whether the candidate you favored was, in fact, the better performer on the logic-based reasoning task.
After all decisions are complete, one of your evaluation decisions will be randomly selected to determine your bonus payment.
Your bonus is based on whether you bet on the right candidate.
Specifically, you can earn a bonus of up to $2. For each set of candidates, you will use

a slider to select any value from 0 to 100 percent, indicating how much you want to bet on the endorsed candidate winning.  If the endorser correctly predicted the better performer, your bonus equals $2 multiplied by your stake percentage. If the endorser incorrectly predicted the better performer, your bonus equals $2 multiplied by 100 minus your stake percent.

Note that endorsers are motivated to provide accurate predictions, because their payment amount depends on the accuracy of their prediction. Moreover, the more you bet on an accurate endorsement, the higher the endorser’s bonus. The lower the amount you bet on their endorsement, the less money the endorser will earn, even if their prediction ends up being correct. In other words, endorsers’ bonuses depend both on their accuracy and on your willingness to bet on them.

You will complete three short tasks today: a word search, a general knowledge quiz, and a pattern logic task. Please work quickly and accurately without using any outside resources (no web searches, notes, or calculators). One of the three tasks will be randomly selected to determine a performance-based bonus; higher performance on that task earns you a larger bonus.

On the next page you’ll see one example with a solution for each task so you can familiarize yourself with the format. The examples are not scored. After the examples, the real tasks begin and each is timed. Once a timer ends, the page will advance automatically and you cannot go back, so please keep an eye on the time.

You will complete three word-search puzzles. You have 90 seconds per puzzle. Each puzzle contains 10 hidden target words, and you will see a list of 30 candidate words below the grid. Check every candidate you believe appears in the grid; leave unchecked any you believe do not.

Your score for this task is based on correct minus incorrect selections, and the task total cannot be negative (so random clicking is discouraged). When the timer ends, the page will move on automatically.

You will answer 48 multiple-choice questions in 4 minutes. Questions cover a mix of topics (e.g., geography, arts, history) and appear in random order. Each question has four options with one correct answer. If you don’t know an answer, make your best guess before time runs out.

You will solve 10 visual pattern problems. Each problem shows a 3×3 matrix with one cell missing. Choose the option (from six possibilities) that best completes the pattern. You have 5 minutes for this task, so work steadily and guess if you’re unsure.
